# Guided tours

These are the app's own tours, written out. To take one in the app, with each control highlighted in turn, choose it under Help > Tours.

## Getting started

1. **The image canvas.** Your layers are drawn here. Scroll to zoom. Drag to rotate or pan; the Rotate and Pan buttons on the toolbar choose which. Double-click to reset the view.
2. **Add a data layer.** New Layer adds data for the time range shown above it. It opens one window with a tab per source: HV (JPEG 2000) for fast Helioviewer images, VSO (FITS) for calibrated files, Direct (FITS) for a mission's own archive, and Local FITS Library for FITS already on this computer. Layers > Open Image Layer opens a file from disk.
3. **The layer list.** Each layer you load gets a row here. When the tour starts on an empty canvas it loads a small bundled sample, an SDO/AIA 171 image from 2012-08-31, so there is one to try. The checkbox shows or hides a layer, and the x removes it. Drag rows to reorder them. Double-click a layer's name to change its dataset.
4. **Layer options.** Select a layer in the list to see its options here (with no layer loaded, this space is empty). Under Display, Color picks the color table. Under Intensity, the two Levels handles set the brightness window.
5. **Play the movie.** Play runs the movie, and the arrows beside it step one frame at a time. Drag the slider to move through time. J, K and L play backward, stop and play forward from anywhere in the window.
6. **Timelines.** This pane plots time series and events against the movie time. Click an empty part of the plot to move the movie to that time. The Timelines button on the toolbar shows or hides the pane.
7. **Projection.** The Projection button opens a palette that changes how the Sun is mapped onto the screen, for example Orthographic or Latitudinal.
8. **Record a movie.** The red dot records the view as a movie; click it again to stop. Under Playback and Recording in the sidebar, choose One loop, Screenshot or Unlimited, and the output size. Files are saved in the Exports folder inside the HFStudio folder in your home folder.
9. **Getting help.** The Help menu in the menu bar holds the Interaction Guide, which lists the mouse and keyboard shortcuts, and the User Manual. Help > Tours runs this tour again and lists the others.

## Loading data

1. **New Layer.** New Layer adds an image layer. Pick a format at the top of its menu: JPEG 2000 for Helioviewer's fast, streamed 8-bit images; FITS (VSO) for calibrated files at full bit depth through the Virtual Solar Observatory; or FITS (native) for a mission's own archive, such as PUNCH, Solar Orbiter, Proba-3 ASPIICS, MLSO or LASCO.
2. **Time step.** The next layer covers the movie's time range, one frame per time step. Tick Frame count to set how many frames instead, and the time step follows. The line under it estimates the video length before anything downloads.
3. **Your layers.** Each layer you load gets a row here. Double-click a layer's name to change its dataset. The checkbox shows or hides a layer, the x removes it, and dragging a row reorders the layers.
4. **Files from disk.** Drop FITS or JPEG 2000 files anywhere on the window to load them as image layers, or use Layers > Open Image Layer. A dropped .jhv file opens that session.
5. **The newest PUNCH day.** Layers > PUNCH Latest opens the newest day of PUNCH clear average mosaics (CAM) in Helioradial with RHEF, in one step.
6. **No data handy?.** Help > Open Demo Scene opens a new session with a bundled SDO/AIA 171 image and RHEF on, so there is something to try with nothing to download.

## Making a movie

1. **Play.** Play runs the movie and the arrows beside it step one frame at a time. Drag the slider to move through time. J, K and L play backward, stop and play forward from anywhere in the window.
2. **Play rate and the end.** Under Playback and Recording, Play sets the rate, in frames per second or in solar minutes, hours or days per second. Loop, Stop and Swing choose what happens when playback reaches the end.
3. **Trim.** Movie > Trim Start Here (I) and Trim End Here (O) set the movie's in and out points at the current frame. Movie > Reset Trim clears them.
4. **What to record.** Record chooses One loop, which records the movie once through; Screenshot, which writes a single still; or Unlimited, which records until you stop it.
5. **Size and format.** Below that are the aspect ratio, the pixels on the long side, and the format: the codec and container, and how much colour detail and bit depth the file keeps. A preset saves a set of these under a name.
6. **Record.** The red dot starts recording with those settings; click it again to stop. Files are saved in the Exports folder inside the HFStudio folder in your home folder.
7. **Quick Share.** File > Quick Share records one loop as a movie that plays anywhere, then shows it in the file manager. Your recording settings are not changed.
8. **Find your movies.** File > Open Exports Folder shows the folder movies, screenshots and metadata are exported to.
9. **Present.** Present shows the output only, full screen, for a talk; Esc leaves. Hold the button for its settings.

## Views and projections

1. **Projection.** Projection opens a palette that changes how the Sun is mapped onto the screen. Orthographic draws it in 3D; HPC, Helioradial and Helioradial Unrolled are flat maps of the sky around it; Latitudinal is a map of the surface.
2. **Warp.** In the Helioradial projections, Warp is the strength of the Box-Cox stretch (lambda): to the right it stretches the inner corona outward, at the left it is the unwarped view.
3. **Crop.** Crop cuts the picture to a disc, in solar radii, and frames that disc without changing the warp. Leftmost is automatic: no crop.
4. **Back to the defaults.** Reset view returns warp, crop and zoom to their defaults.
5. **Camera.** Camera sets where the view is seen from: Free, from the active image layer's observer; Follow, from a selected object; or Overview, down on the solar equatorial plane. It can also revolve the camera about an axis.
6. **Track solar rotation.** Track keeps the view turning with the Sun as the movie plays; Differential, beside it, toggles differential rotation.
7. **Multiview.** Multiview puts each shown image layer in a view of its own, side by side.
8. **Compare.** Compare blinks between two image layers, or swipes a divider across the view with one on each side. Layers > Duplicate Layer gives you a copy of a layer to compare against.
9. **Pizza.** Pizza cuts every shown image layer into its own wedges or tiles of one Sun. The wedges follow solar north, so they stay on the Sun as the camera moves; in Helioradial Unrolled they become strips.
10. **Grid and overlays.** Grid holds the coordinate grid, the solar limb, the Thomson and celestial spheres, the ecliptic plane and the planets, each with its own colour, opacity and width.
11. **Reset View.** Reset View returns the view to its default; double-clicking the canvas does the same.

## RHEF and filters

1. **The Filters palette.** Filters opens a palette for one layer. RHEF, the radial histogram equalizing filter, comes first and works frame by frame. Below it, the Fourier filter and the noise gate work over the whole movie.
2. **RHEF in the layer options.** Select a layer in the list and open Intensity: its Filter row is the same RHEF switch, bound to the same setting. When the tour starts on an empty canvas it loads the bundled SDO/AIA 171 sample, so there is a layer to try. The Υ button beside the list stays greyed until RHEF is chosen. Then it opens Shadows (Υ low) and Highlights (Υ high), which soften RHEF output below and above the median, each on its own; a curve that shows their shape; a Look menu; and Hold to compare, which shows that one layer without RHEF while you hold it.
3. **Reading an RHEF image.** RHEF output is a visualization, not a calibrated radiance. Measure on the original data, with the filter set to None. The method is described in Gilly & Cranmer 2025.
4. **Find a filter by name.** Help > Search Controls finds any control by name. Try noise gate, or RHEF.

## Sharing your work

1. **Save the session.** File > Save Session writes the whole scene, its layers and settings, to a .jhv file that opens it again later.
2. **Your own starting scene.** File > Set Current Session as Default opens this scene at every start, ahead of the last session. File > Clear Default Session undoes it.
3. **Share Scene.** File > Share Scene saves the scene for someone else: your home folder is written as ~, and local files outside the cache are listed first.
4. **Take the data too.** File > Export Session with Data saves the session plus a .data.zip of its local files, to open on another computer.
5. **Copy Provenance.** File > Copy Provenance puts the program, its build and each layer's data source on the clipboard, for a caption or a methods section.
6. **Copy Frame.** Edit > Copy Frame puts the canvas picture on the clipboard, as an 8-bit screenshot.
7. **Send to Python.** Layers > Send to Python writes the active layer's FITS files as double-precision science FITS, plus a manifest and a sunpy snippet.
8. **SAMP.** SAMP sends a message to other astronomy tools that speak SAMP, the Virtual Observatory's messaging protocol.
